en: The Buddha-Spoken Mahāvaipulya Skillful Means Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and sixteen thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom were fully endowed with wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers; who possessed unimpeded eloquence and had attained the great dhāraṇīs.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the great Dharma-seat, surrounded with reverence by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of beings such as these, who listened to and received his preaching of the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Jñānottara. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
Having completed the prostrations, he joined his palms, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have a minor matter I wish to pose as a question to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Out of compassion for me, I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottara, saying: “Good son!
Ask whatever you wish; now is precisely the right time.”
“The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in accordance with those who inquire, each expound the Dharma for them as is appropriate, so that upon hearing it, their hearts give rise to joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
We pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain this in detail.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Jñānottara, saying:
“Good son! You should now know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means causes all sentient beings everywhere to practice according to the principle through a single expedient.”

Why is this? Because a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva endowed with skillful means, even toward those of different species among the animals and within the various evil destinies, employs skillful means with a mind of universal omniscience that is equal toward all; he then dedicates these roots of goodness to all sentient beings, causing them to practice two dharmas.
What are these two? They are:
the mind of omniscience and the mind of dedication.
“Good son! This is called the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!”

A bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means does not harbor thoughts of destroying any of the roots of goodness possessed by sentient beings; rather, always cherishing them, they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) and dedicates those roots of goodness born from such sympathetic joy to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, with the mind of omniscience, one extensively bestows gifts upon all sentient beings; yet, although the intention to give arises, there is nothing grasped and nothing attained. Good son!
This is called the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,

whenever a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means goes to those worlds of the ten directions, or even to all other places, he may see all kinds of exquisite and lovely fragrant trees and flowering trees.
Having seen them, the bodhisattva does not give rise to a single thought of desire to take them, but reflects thus:
"These fragrance trees and flower trees are not for my own taking; they shall be offered to all the Buddhas of the ten directions."
He then dedicates such roots of goodness toward all-knowledge.
Son of good family!
This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva endowed with skillful means encounters any place where all sentient beings are experiencing various forms of happiness, the bodhisattva then gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedicates these roots of goodness born from such sympathetic joy toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva, wherever he may go, sees all sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, he then gives rise to a heart of compassion and pity, dons the armor of diligence, and speaks these words:
"I shall take upon myself all the sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings; I universally vow that all beings may attain peace and happiness."
He then dedicates these roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi. Noble son,
this is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means, wherever he may be, when he pays homage to a single Buddha-Tathāgata, it is equivalent to paying homage to all those Buddha-Tathāgatas."

Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas share the same dharma-nature; they share the same categories of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and they likewise share the same supreme mental intention.

Once the Bodhisattva has understood this, even if they reverently make offerings to but a single Buddha-Tathāgata, it is equivalent to reverently making offerings to all Buddha-Tathāgatas; for the Bodhisattva universally embraces all beings with a vast mind.
"Good son! This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!"

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva endowed with skillful means occasionally sees one practicing the Mahāyāna who has developed a mind of regression and despondency toward the Mahāyāna Dharma, the Bodhisattva, having understood that person's mind, immediately reflects:
"I should praise for them a single four-line verse, causing them to practice and study in accordance with the principle so that they do not regress."
Having reflected thus, he immediately said:

"All those who cultivate the Mahāyāna, if they can understand the meaning of this four-line verse, will be able to penetrate the significance of all speech; as they have understood it, they shall not fall back or sink."
Furthermore, regarding this four-line verse that I have spoken, if there are those who are able to hear and receive it, such persons shall immediately attain the eloquence of all Buddhas.

By means of these roots of goodness, I shall universally bestow them upon all sentient beings, and I vow that they shall all come to possess the abundant learning and the unimpeded eloquence of the Buddhas, which is encompassed by all-encompassing wisdom.
“Good son! This is called the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means occasionally goes to those who are poor and begging, the bodhisattva then gives rise to a heart of compassion and thinks to himself:
"The actions performed by others result in determinate retribution; I shall now joyfully and harmoniously accord with their desires and bestow everything upon them."
As the Buddha has taught, there are four aspects within a single act of giving, namely:
the greatness of the gift, the greatness of the mind, and so forth.
Although the gift I offer here is small, my mind directed toward omniscience is immeasurable.

If I give this to this beggar with a mind of omniscience, then by the power of such roots of goodness, may my jewel-hand constantly produce precious treasures to bestow universally upon all sentient beings.

In this way, giving to such a beggar is equal and no different from the meritorious deeds performed by those who give to, observe the precepts for, and practice meditative concentration under the present Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
“Good son! This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!”

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva endowed with skillful means dwells together with those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, at that time the Bodhisattva conceives only reverence toward those followers of the two vehicles.
If those śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas give rise to the notion of a self by means of two things, what are these two?
First, that bodhisattvas give birth to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; second, that the Buddhas give birth to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He thinks to himself regarding this matter:
"I am the most superior among these; how could I possibly give rise to a mind of reverence toward them?
Yet, although this bodhisattva hears such words, through skillful means his mind remains free from such divergent thoughts.
"Good son! This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means is able to accomplish the six pāramitās within a single act of giving.
What are these characteristics?
They are as follows:

Whenever a bodhisattva encounters a supplicant in any place, he at that time subdues his stingy mind and bestows everything according to the other's wishes; this is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).

When practicing such giving, the bodhisattva maintains the precepts themselves and is further able to gather those who have broken the precepts, causing them all to dwell securely in the ground of pure ethical discipline; this is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
When giving in this manner, the bodhisattva takes a mind of loving-kindness as primary, further giving rise to a non-destructive mind, a mind of protection, and a mind of equanimity.
When these minds arise, this is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

When practicing such giving—whether of drink, food, or whatever else is desired—the Bodhisattva experiences no weariness or fatigue in the states of body, speech, and mind as they come, go, stay, or rest according to what is given; this is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing such giving, the bodhisattva’s mind dwells on a single object and does not give rise to distraction, regardless of the recipient; this is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
When practicing such giving, the bodhisattva fully knows the giver, the recipient, and what kind of karmic fruit is obtained.

Having known this, they weigh and calculate all things as being entirely equal; therein, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended. This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Good son! In this way, it is called the skillful means by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the six pāramitās within a single act of giving."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottama again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

Within the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s giving, there exists such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); by means of these skillful means, they are able to liberate all sentient beings from the suffering and affliction of saṃsāra and universally encompass the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha said:
“Jñānottara! It is just as you have said; it is so, it is so.”
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they are able to accomplish immeasurable superior practices for the benefit of others within a single act of giving.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottara, saying: "Good son,

you should now know that even if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva endowed with skillful means should at some other time commit an extremely grave offense, that Bodhisattva nevertheless does not destroy their roots of goodness."
How is it that they do not fall away? It is as follows:

when a bodhisattva occasionally encounters an evil friend who exhorts them to retreat from and lose the resolve for the unsurpassed path, and thereby incurs extremely grave offenses, the bodhisattva at that time reflects to themselves:

"If I were now to realize nirvana within this very body and bring an end to the cycle of existence, I would no longer be able to don the armor of diligence; how then could I deliver all sentient beings from the suffering and afflictions of saṃsāra?"
I should not now allow my mind to be ruined by this circumstance. Why is this?
It is because I desire to deliver all sentient beings from saṃsāra; even if I were to commit an extremely grave offense, I would still not sever my roots of goodness.
"Good son! This is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a renunciant bodhisattva gives rise to a discriminating mind and forms divergent mental orientations, the transgression they incur exceeds that of the four root downfalls.
If such a bodhisattva possesses skillful means, they shall repent immediately upon its arising. Good son!
"I declare that such a bodhisattva is one who is without fault.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How can it be that a bodhisattva also incurs transgressions?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottara, saying: "Good son!
If it is said that a bodhisattva is without fault, how is it that a bodhisattva, having trained in the prātimokṣa precepts for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, might break the root fruit?

"Good son! You should now know that although these bodhisattvas are able to endure both kind and harsh words from all sentient beings, they nevertheless apply their mental attention in accordance with the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, I say that the transgressions they incur are greater than those of the four root downfalls."
Just as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, having committed a root offense, are no longer capable of attaining realization of Nirvāṇa;

so too it is with a renunciant Bodhisattva who, having given rise to such an offense, does not immediately repent and abandon the mental orientations associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—they likewise become incapable and cannot proceed to realize the realm of Great Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was present in the great assembly and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the great city of Śrāvastī, there is a bodhisattva named Prabhūtarāja."
On one occasion, when I entered the city to beg for alms, I did not see that bodhisattva within the city.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Light-Assembly was staying separately in another village, sitting in the same place as a woman and speaking improper words.
When I went there and saw him, he did not conceal anything, yet he spoke of the dharma of the holy life in a different way.
World-Honored One!
You, the Buddha Tathāgata, are the Great Teacher of all sentient beings; there is nothing you do not know, nothing you do not see, and nothing you do not understand.
"I see this sign; what is its significance?
I pray that the Buddha will reveal it to me.
When the Venerable Ānanda spoke these words, the earth beneath this assembly of the Buddha shook violently.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Massed Radiance manifested his body in the air at a height of one tala tree, and from mid-air he addressed Ānanda, saying: "Venerable Ānanda!
"What do you think?
Can one who has committed an unrighteous act abide thus in empty space?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, facing the empty space before the Tathāgata, asked:
“Bodhisattva King of the Mass of Light!
Regarding the signs and phenomena I previously observed, how could a bodhisattva possess such unrighteousness?
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, the World-Honored One immediately extended his foot and pressed it upon the ground.
At that time, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appeared in the void from another world and uttered these words:
"The Bodhisattva has already departed from what is not the Dharma; I know this matter, I have realized this matter."
When that Buddha had finished speaking, he vanished from the sky and did not appear again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should not conceive thoughts of fault toward those who abide in the Mahāyāna, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Ānanda! Just as those in the Śrāvaka vehicle who have attained the first two fruits find it no difficulty to seek the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), so too it is for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who possess skillful means (upāya-kauśalya): they find it no difficulty to seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has already become free from the entanglements of kin and family, and is able to dwell securely in the unshakable pure faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, never regressing from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Ānanda, you should know that if there is one who abides in the Bodhisattva vehicle and does not depart from the mind of omniscience, even if they engage in the play of the five desires, they commit no transgression.
That all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, attain the perfection of the five faculties is explained by this principle.
"Ānanda! Regarding the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Raśmiprabhāsasamudgatarāja as you have seen them, I shall now explain them to you in accordance with reality."
Ānanda! You should now know that as for the woman who was sitting together with the Bodhisattva Prabhūtarāja in the village, she was once his wife during two hundred previous lifetimes.
Therefore, at this time, this woman beheld the auspicious and majestic radiance, as well as the precepts and power, of the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-rāja-saṃcaya.
Having seen him, due to her past habitual tendencies, she conceived a coarse and heavy notion; yet, by the power of her roots of goodness, she further thought:
"If I could have this Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-rāja-saṃcaya come to my house and sit together with me in one place, he would enable me to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"Ānanda! Then, the Bodhisattva King of the Mass of Light, having known the thoughts in that woman's mind, went to her house during the night and sat together with the woman in one place, extensively proclaiming for her countless Dharma gates."
At that time, the interior and exterior of the woman’s house were level, vast, and magnificently pure.
Once the Bodhisattva King Light-Cluster had taken his seat together with her, he took the woman’s right hand and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha does not praise the dharma of defiled desire, yet the foolish, deluded, and attached practice it.”
"If one can sever the heart of desire and attachment, the Buddha says that such a person is supreme.

"Ānanda! At that time, having heard this verse, the woman was filled with great joy. She immediately rose from her seat, joined her palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva King of the Mass of Light, and spoke this verse:"
“I originally had no mind that truly sought desire; I know that the Buddha does not praise the nature of desire.
If one can sever the heart of craving for desire, the Buddha says such a person is supreme.”
Having spoken these verses, he further spoke in verse:
"You should know that what I have contemplated in my mind Is spoken truly and without deviation.
If any person seeks the Bodhi of the Buddha, All sentient beings shall obtain benefit and happiness."

"Ānanda! At that time, because the Bodhisattva King of the Mass of Light had skillfully employed expedient means to guide her, that woman immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Then that bodhisattva rose from his seat and departed from that house.
"Ānanda! You should know now that I have observed this woman’s profound mind to be pure, courageous, and most excellent; I shall now bestow upon her the prediction of enlightenment."
Ānanda! After that woman passes away from this life, she shall transform her female body and become a man;
thereafter, after ninety-nine hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, she shall attain Buddhahood, appearing in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Upāsaka.
Ānanda! For this reason, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already become free from the entanglements of affection for their kin; all that is unrighteous shall never arise again.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhūtaratnarāja descended from mid-air, touched his head to the ground, and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Having performed his prostrations, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who possesses skillful means dwells in the practice of great compassion and constantly brings benefit to others."
"World-Honored One!
I have now also attained this practice.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If there is a bodhisattva who can cause even a single sentient being to give rise to a single root of goodness, they will not give rise to a sinful mind regarding attachment to form.
If one were to give rise to such a mind of sinful defilement, they would have to undergo the sufferings of hell for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
“World-Honored One!

If that bodhisattva gives rise to such a sinful mind and undergoes this suffering of hell, you should know that this bodhisattva has abandoned the roots of goodness generated for the sake of sentient beings, causing those roots of goodness to be unable to reach fulfillment.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva King of Light-Assembly, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! It is just so, it is just so, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, as you have spoken."
One who dwells in the mind of great compassion is able to sever all stains of sin for all sentient beings. Good son!
I recall that in the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a māṇavaka named Prabhāsa who practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) for forty-two thousand years, remaining free from all faults.
After these forty-two thousand years had passed, on one occasion, due to certain causes and conditions, he entered a royal city named Abhijñā; there, within that city, he saw a woman named Kāṭhā.

At that time, the woman saw that the māṇavaka was handsome and possessed of excellent physical features; having seen him, she conceived a heart of lustful desire, approached him, paid her respects, and stood before him.
"O King of Radiant Masses!
At that time, the māṇavaka asked that woman,
'What is it that you, a woman, seek now?'"
The woman replied, "I now seek you, māṇavaka, to be my husband. The māṇavaka said:
"I do not give rise to thoughts of desire for women.
The woman spoke again:
"If I do not obtain you as my husband at this time, I shall soon meet my end."
At that time, the māṇavaka thought to himself:

"For forty-two thousand years I have practiced the holy life and not transgressed the prohibitions; at this present moment, I ought not to accept such unrighteous defilement and passion, and I should distance myself from this woman."
Having formed this thought, he departed from that woman and walked seven paces.
Having gone those seven paces, he paused once more and, conceiving a heart of great compassion for the woman, thought to himself:

"At this moment, I shall arouse a courageous and resolute mind; even if I were to violate the prohibitive precepts, I would rather endure the retribution of suffering in hell than allow her to lose her life by abandoning her."
At that time, having heard these words, the woman felt joy arise in her heart; her original wish was fulfilled before her life came to an end.
King Prabhūtaratna! Then that boy, the mass of light, took the hand of that woman Gaṭā and spoke these words:
"As you desire, I shall now do for you whatever is appropriate.
Thus, the youth Prabhāsa and the woman Ghaṭā lived together as husband and wife for twelve years.
After those twelve years had passed, that māṇavaka again practiced the holy life with diligence; having died thereafter, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.
"Rāśirāja! You should now know this: do not entertain any doubt that the youth Prabhāsa at that time was anyone other than my own self;
and the woman Gaṭā at that time was none other than Yaśodharā."
Why is this? At that time, I was only able to give rise to a single thought of great compassion; furthermore, by once again practicing the holy life, I attained rebirth in the Brahma realm.
In this way, throughout ten thousand kalpas, I have received bodies within saṃsāra; though I have received these bodies, I have never felt weariness or revulsion.
King Raśmisaṃcaya!
Those sentient beings who lack skillful means undergo the sufferings of the hells within saṃsāra.
Because the bodhisattva is able to fulfill skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he is therefore born in the Brahma realm.
"King Radiant Cluster!
Even if Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were great arhats whose supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom were foremost among the śrāvakas, they still could not fully possess skillful means."
"King of Radiant Masses!
Now, within my Dharma there is a bhikṣu named Kokālika who has fallen into hell; what are the circumstances of this?"
"King of Radiant Masses!
I recall that in the past, during the Dharma of Krakucchanda Buddha, there was a bhikṣu named Vimala.
At that time, that bhikṣu practiced the araṇā conduct, dwelling alone in a single rock cave."
Not far from that cliff, there was a separate dwelling where a rishi possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) resided.
Suddenly, at one time, he spread a great black cloud and sent down a torrential rain.
Then, that nearby rishi possessing the five supernatural powers went to the cliff-dwelling of the bhikṣu Vimala, desiring to cause him distress and harm, and to destroy his holy life (brahmacarya).
At that time, as the ṛṣi was entering, the bhikṣu was just leaving.
Upon seeing him, the ṛṣi gave rise to a defiled mind and falsely conceived a disparaging thought, thinking:
"This stainless bhikṣu has fallen away from the holy life and intends to commit an unrighteous act."
At that time, having understood the thoughts in the mind of that seer, the bhikṣu immediately leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
Seeing the bhikṣu stationed in mid-air, the seer said:
"I have brought this sharp blade here to this crag to destroy your holy life; why do you now remain suspended in the air?"
When the seer had finished speaking, the bhikṣu immediately descended from the air and prostrated before the seer, no longer leaping upward.
At that moment, the seer’s entire body fell in an instant into that great hell.
"Rāśiprabha! What do you think?
Do not harbor any doubt that the stainless bhikṣu of that time was anyone other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya."
That rishi with the five supernormal powers was none other than the bhikṣu Kokālika.
King Prabhūtaratna!
You should know that this causal connection is not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is entirely the sphere of activity for the skillful means and wisdom of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"King Prabhāsa! Furthermore, it is like a person in the world named Gaṇika who is fully endowed with sixty-four kinds of arts and skills.
This person loves wealth and treasures; wherever he goes, by virtue of his arts and skills, he is able to obtain everything he requires."
Just as one might receive wealth and profit from various individuals and later forget their kindness, giving rise to a mind of abandonment, so too is the Bodhisattva endowed with skillful means:
although he employs every kind of expedient to rescue and deliver sentient beings in all places, he harbors no expectations or desires for anything from those beings toward whom he acts.

Seeing the roots of goodness possessed by those sentient beings, he exhorts them to increase and advance them; by the power of the roots of goodness thus performed, he causes all sentient beings everywhere to give rise to superior practices, while the Bodhisattva himself remains free from any attachment.
Even regarding matters such as play and amusement, although he may engage in them for the sake of others, he has already relinquished them and no longer allows them to bind his mind.
“King Prabhūtaratna!

Furthermore, it is like various species of animals in the world who, upon seeing a magnificent flower endowed with exquisite color and fragrance, are unable to give rise to even a single thought of affection or delight.

It is the same for a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means: although they may experience all manner of playful pleasures and such, they never give rise to even a single thought of attachment or delight; there is nothing self-made and nothing made by another, for they are entirely without clinging.
"King of Radiant Masses!
Furthermore, just as when seeds are planted in soil that is rich and fertile, they will certainly produce sprouts, stalks, and fruits;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva who possesses skillful means. By cultivating the liberation gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he is certainly able to remain free from all defiled dharmas. Although he may experience all manner of worldly pleasures and diversions, he does not impair his cultivation of the meritorious accomplishments praised by the Buddhas."
“King Prabhūtaratna!
It is just as when a fisherman in the world sets a large net across a great pond to catch fish; whatever he desires, he is able to take up entirely, without letting them fall back into the water.”

It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means: practicing the liberation gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, protected by the firm resolve for omniscience, they ultimately do not fall into the mire of birth and death; rather, having extinguished this body in various places, they are reborn in the Brahma realm.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Dharma Master Śīladharma, recipient of the purple robe and subject, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, King of Light-Clusters!
It is also like a vidyādhara who has well cultivated the siddhi-dharmas of yoga and is bound within the five secret fetters; yet, according to the rites he performs, he does not transgress samādhi."
By the power of a single great mantra-phrase, this person is able to sever all those bonds and attain stable abiding in the gateway of secret practice.
Although remaining within bondage, they never depart from samādhi.

It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses skillful means: though they sport and act in accordance with the objects of the five desires, their correct practice remains unimpaired by whatever they do.
By the power of the light of this single wisdom, this bodhisattva is able to completely purify all defiled dharmas and can abide securely in the mind of omniscience.
Although they experience the pleasures of the five desires, they are constantly born in the Brahma heavens.
“King Prabhūtaratna!
It is just as when someone in the world who is skilled with the sword is expert and proficient in its techniques.
This person once conceals his sharp blade and travels alone through the wilderness and perilous places.”
On the way, he suddenly saw a man who was alone without a companion and possessed no weapons.
When the sword-wielder saw that man, a heart of compassion arose within him;
he immediately drew near and said to him, "You are now traveling alone, with no companion at all and no weapons; how will you protect yourself?"
"You shall now accompany me wherever I go; I will never allow you to suffer any lack or loss.
Should you suddenly encounter robbers or other such dangers, I shall provide you with great protection."
Having spoken thus, they traveled together.

On the way, they suddenly encountered a band of robbers; at that time, the fellow travelers did not know that this man had previously concealed a sharp sword, and upon seeing the robbers, they were immediately struck with fear.
At that time, the man with the sword gave rise to a courageous and fierce mind; free from any fear or trepidation, he immediately drew his sword and engaged in combat against the bandits.
He then took the lives of all those bandits. Having protected himself, he was further able to shield his companions, so that they all reached safety and passed through this perilous difficulty.

It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means: though they possess various kinds of expedients and wield the sword of wisdom, even while sporting and acting in accordance with the objects of the five desires, they never for a moment allow the faculty of the body to give rise to negligence, but are able to provide great protection for that faculty of the body.

Even if they encounter the demon of afflictions at another time, the bodhisattva likewise remains unmoved; donning the armor of diligence, they give rise to no fear, severing the net of afflictions with the sword of wisdom and rendering them entirely pure.
"Bodhisattvas are always born in pure buddha-fields.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Kāmadarśin, who at the time of his meal entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, the Bodhisattva proceeded in due order until he reached the house of a certain elder. He stood by the side of the gate and raised his voice to beg for alms.
The elder had a daughter named Uttara-dhana, who was of upright countenance and beloved by all who beheld her.
At that time, upon hearing the voice of the Bodhisattva, the woman took food and drink and went out to offer it to him.

Having given him the food, she immediately conceived a sense of affection and delight toward the Bodhisattva; through attachment to his physical form and his voice, she gave rise to a mind of lustful passion due to these causes and conditions.
When the Bodhisattva Kāmadarśana saw this woman, he immediately knew her thoughts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had no intention toward the dharma of lustful attachment, and he reflected to himself:
"To give rise to even a single thought of lustful attachment for a mere moment would be a grave transgression."
Why is this? Regarding this woman, from what source could I have conceived such affection?
If it were her visual faculty that is the object of affection, the eye is impermanent, subject to decay, and a mass of impure flesh; its intrinsic nature is empty—what is there to find delight in?

If the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-faculties are considered lovable, then those respective faculties are likewise so; their intrinsic nature is entirely empty and devoid of any substantial reality—what, then, is there to love or delight in?

In this way, from the feet to the crown of the head, and even throughout the internal, external, and intermediate [parts], one examines each according to reality with thorough discernment; therein, not even the slightest dharma can be found.
Having now contemplated in this way according to reality, I see that all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
Because phenomena do not exist, they are without arising.
When the Bodhisattva engaged in such reflection, he immediately attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Having obtained this benefit, the bodhisattva’s heart was filled with great joy; he immediately leaped from that spot into the air to the height of a *tāla* tree, circumambulated the city seven times to the right, departed from the great city of Śrāvastī, and traveling through the sky, approached the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the Bodhisattva Kṛtaprema approaching slowly through the air with sovereign ease, his majestic power as towering as that of a king of geese.
Having seen him, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!
“Do you see this Bodhisattva Love-Maker (Priyadarśana) coming through the air?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Yes, I have seen it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“You should now know that this bodhisattva has become free from craving and attachment toward all phenomena; having realized the non-arising of dharmas and attained nothing at all, he is able to subdue all demonic armies and extensively turn the wheel of the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking, that bodhisattva immediately remained in mid-air to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the woman Uttara suddenly passed away at the house of the elder and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; she transformed her female form and obtained the body of a devaputra.
When that devaputra was born, a magnificent palace adorned with the seven precious jewels appeared simultaneously, measuring twelve yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, a retinue of fourteen thousand celestial maidens was born at the same time.
In an instant, these goddesses developed their own wisdom and all thought to themselves:
"By what roots of goodness have we now been born here?"
He immediately knew:
"In a previous life, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was the daughter of an elder who conceived a defiled, lustful attachment toward a bodhisattva.
By this cause and condition, she passed away from that life and was reborn here among the devas, transforming her female form into that of a deva-son."
"He has attained immeasurable, supreme retributive powers and supernormal knowledges; because of these superior causes and conditions of this devaputra, we too have been born here.
Having had this thought, they dwelt there filled with joy.
At that time, the newly born deva-son had this thought:
"In my former life among humans, I gave rise to a mind of stained attachment; how is it that I have now obtained such a superior retribution?"
This causal condition is due to the superior power of the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana acting as a guide.

I should now proceed to the place where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, resides, to pay respectful offerings to that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and to behold and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana.

At that time, having formed this thought, the devaputra immediately took various kinds of exquisite and wonderful incense and flowers, accompanied by his retinue of celestial maidens, and came from that celestial realm to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One; then, before the Buddha, he joined his palms toward the sky and paid distant homage to the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Thereafter, he respectfully and reverently offered the various incenses, flowers, and other items he had brought to the World-Honored One.
Having made these offerings, he circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke this verse:
"Inconceivable Honored One among Men!
Inconceivable Great Enlightenment!"
Inconceivable are the practices of all Buddhas!
Inconceivable are the dharmas of all Buddhas!
I am the daughter of a householder in the city of Śrāvastī; my father originally gave me the name Uttara-dhana.
His physical appearance was so dignified and majestic that all held him in high esteem; his parents and kinsmen also cherished him with affection.
At one time, there was a son of the Buddha, endowed with great majesty and virtue, named Priya.
While wandering for alms in the city of Śrāvastī, he came in due course to my house.
At that time, hearing those beautiful sounds, I was filled with delight and joy, and immediately took the food;
carrying the food, I went before him with affection and, with a heart of deep respect, offered it to the Son of the Buddha.
At that time, seeing those wondrous forms and features, my heart gave rise to passionate attachment and the desire for union;
yet because of those causes and conditions, it could not be accomplished, and in an instant, my life was cut short.

I cannot now fully proclaim it all; yet by creating the great causal conditions for becoming a beloved son of the Buddha, one becomes disassociated from the phenomena of defiled attachment, so that after my passing, I may be born in a superior realm.
World-Honored One!
Although I have cast off my former retribution, how joyful it is that my female form has been severed; I have been transformed into a man of great majestic radiance.
Furthermore, I have been reborn in the celestial realm, where fourteen thousand goddesses born together with me serve as my retinue.
Furthermore, there appeared simultaneously most sublime adornments of the seven treasures and a wondrous, subtle palace.
At that time, such a thought arose in me: "This is an inconceivable matter;
how is it that by taking a mind of defiled attachment as the cause, I have obtained this pure retribution?"
To act as a beloved son of the Buddha is most rare; it is also called "Acting with Joy" and "Acting with Radiance.
My own body blazes with great majesty and light, having obtained such [a state] through those supreme causes.
The cause of defilement can produce such a fruit, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know;
for this teaching does not exist within their vehicles, but only the wisdom of the Sugata can turn it.

Even if one were to spend eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, unable to cultivate and study the wisdom of all Buddhas, I now have no other aspiration in my heart; I seek only the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha-son Maitreya of great majesty is my supreme spiritual friend;
because of him, I have been able to see the Buddha and abide securely in bodhi without regression.
I know that those who practice for enlightenment have no attachment to a mind stained by desire;
just as I have transformed this female form, may all beings everywhere likewise become men.
In a previous life, after my life had ended, my parents and kinsmen were gripped by grief and distress;
their hearts were so entangled by the extreme suffering of their affection that they instead gave rise to anger toward the śramaṇa.
Now, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I have arrived at my father’s abode in a single instant;
concealing my form as I dwell in the air, I address him:
"Do not give rise to anger toward the śramaṇa; for one who gives rise to anger incurs great fault and will suffer affliction throughout the long night."

The daughter of the wealthy man was I myself; having been born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, I have transformed that female form of my previous retribution and attained the body of a Great Radiance Devaputra.
Parents, you should now go to the presence of the Buddha and repent for that mind of anger;
the Buddha is the great compassionate father of all sentient beings, the refuge to which all sentient beings turn.
Having heard the sound of the Buddha’s voice, their parents immediately gave rise to a vast and superior resolve;
at that moment, sustained by the Buddha's power, they proceeded at once to the Buddha’s abode as soon as the words were spoken.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, repented for having previously given rise to a mind of anger and resentment, and said:
“I now take refuge in the Buddha.”
Joining his palms, he again asked:
"The Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are most supreme; how should one perform acts of offering to them?"
"Only the Buddha can know my thoughts and intentions; as I have asked, may the Buddha please explain.
Having spoken these words, he remained in sincere composure, listening with single-minded longing and veneration.
The Buddha addressed the parents of Uttara-dhana, saying:
“Listen now attentively to what I say: if you wish to make offerings to all the Buddhas, you should give rise to the bodhicitta.”
You should know that your daughter, Uttarakāśyapā, has planted roots of goodness throughout five hundred lifetimes;
she has now transformed her female body to become a son of heaven, acting as a skillful guide for you, her parents.
When the parents heard these words of the Buddha, they immediately gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
filled with joy, they praised him, saying:
"The Great Sage among men speaks according to reality."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You now bear witness to such matters: the inconceivable skillful means of a bodhisattva, by which a pure retribution is obtained even from a defiled mind."
Just as these signs were manifested by the woman Vāsavadattā, so it is with all sentient beings, Ānanda!
Such supreme merit is able to cause all sentient beings to be free from suffering.
Now this son of heaven, through his superior karmic reward, remains ever pure despite his affectionate heart;
he is able to revere the Buddha, the World-Honored One, because he honors unsurpassed bodhi.
Having made offerings to Buddhas throughout many eons, And having planted roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas,
Firmly abiding in the bodhicitta, One shall certainly attain the fruit of enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

According to my understanding, it is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is composed of various jewels; although these various jewels possess various colors, it is the golden color that is supreme among them."

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: whether it be a pure mind, a defiled mind, a mind dwelling on phenomena, or a mind concealing phenomena—though these various minds differ in such ways, the mind of omniscience is supreme among them all.
World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first abide securely in the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), whereby they are able to purify all defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*).
It is like a medicine called "Excellent Manifestation" (*Sudarśana*), which can cure all the sufferings of disease in the world.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the mind of omniscience, they are able to eliminate all the diseases of affliction, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, Ānanda!
It is just as you have said; it is so, it is so."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
That Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to practice the supreme path of tranquility, and are able to give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, constantly benefiting them.”

Furthermore, they are able to cultivate the liberation gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they take no pleasure in the dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they do not depart from the mind of omniscience in any circumstance; and they possess inconceivable skillful means.

"Bhagavān! All the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unattached and unimpeded; they act within the spheres of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles without grasping, nor do they give rise to any conditioned activity."
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to employ a parable to clarify the conduct of a bodhisattva; I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will grant me permission to speak.
The Buddha said:
“Mahākāśyapa! You should speak with eloquence; now is precisely the right time. Mahākāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were in the world a multitude of hundreds of thousands of people who, in a vast wilderness or a place of perilous difficulty, see a single gate; at that time, each person from within that multitude enters through that gate.”
Having passed through this gate, they next see a road; that road is vast and desolate, perilous and fraught with many hardships.
Upon seeing this road, all those people give rise to fear.
At that time, there was a wise man endowed with skillful means who, desiring to bring benefit and peace to many people, addressed the assembly, saying:
"You should know that not far from here there is a great city."
That city was vast and expansive, magnificent, pure, and serene;
its population was flourishing, and it was peaceful, secure, and abundant.
Those who entered that city experienced perfect joy and happiness.
"Who would delight in entering this city, whereby they may immediately distance themselves from perilous difficulties and terrors?
At that time, a certain class of people among the multitude, having heard these words, immediately spoke:
"I now wish to enter."

Having entered this city, he saw that it was abundant, peaceful, and joyful; conceiving a sense of wonder, he became attached to it and would not leave, remaining there and no longer desiring to go out.
There is a class of people who, upon hearing a description of that city, immediately say:
"I too shall follow and enter that city.
Although these people enter, they do not delight in dwelling there and subsequently return and depart once more.
Furthermore, among the multitude there was a class of people who, although they heard these words, were unable to go forward and enter that city.
"World-Honored One!
Those wise people, having passed beyond this city, must again travel through a wilderness on a perilous path."
Having emerged from this road, he sees a narrow path, only a cubit in width.

On the left side of the path is a great pit a hundred thousand cubits deep, and on the right side of the path is another great pit a hundred thousand cubits deep; if anyone should fall into these pits, they would be unable to escape.
Along that narrow path, in each of the four directions, there was a group of people who cried out:
"I am struck with great terror here!
Furthermore, not far from that narrow path, there was a crossroads where a multitude of people traveled; wherever they turned, they were all able to see a great city.
Just as they see it, each according to their own inclination, gives rise to attachment and delight.
Then that wise person, having seen this narrow path, proceeds along it and reaches a place of safety.
“World-Honored One!
You should know that the countless hundreds of thousands of people in the world are none other than foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
‘One gate’ should be known as grasping at a single personal existence (*eka-ātmabhāva*);”
That one sees a road within that wilderness of peril and difficulty should be understood as the perilous path of birth and death;
that the road is steep and vast should be understood as being caused by ignorance and craving for existence, because the resulting fruit is exceedingly remote.
One who possesses wisdom and is able to lead others should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means;
that great city is none other than the nirvāṇa realized by those of the two vehicles.

There is a class of people who enter that great city, take delight in it, and dwell there peacefully, seeking no way out; you should know that these are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whose resolve is inferior, and who conceive the notion of cessation.

There is another class of people who likewise wish to follow and enter that city, yet do not take pleasure in dwelling there and subsequently emerge; you should know that these are other bodhisattvas, for they have accomplished the mind of supreme resolve.

There is yet another class of people who, despite hearing these words, are unable to advance and enter the city; you should know that these are the various followers of external paths, who possess little merit and lack wisdom.

That wise person who, having passed beyond this city, further emerges from that wilderness path should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with skillful means, by virtue of the perfection of diligence.
That narrow path measuring one foot in width should be known as the supreme dharmadhātu;
the pit on the left side should be known as the stage of the śrāvakas;
and the pit on the right side should be known as the stage of the pratyekabuddhas.
As for those people on all four sides who raise cries of fear, you should know that they are the devas, the Māra-king, and the retinues of Māra;
as for that crossroads, it is the Dharma-gate of the Four Means of Integration (saṃgrahavastu).

Regarding the statement that "whichever direction they turn, they are all able to see a great city," one should know that this refers to those of the two vehicles who, according to their respective capacities, perceive the merits of the Buddha, the Buddha's conduct, and the Buddha's wisdom, thereby giving rise to love and joy.
Regarding the statement that "at that time, those wise people reach a place of peace and security," one should know that this refers to reaching the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
“World-Honored One!

It should be known that such metaphors as these spoken by the Buddha are all the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas to guide sentient beings; this constitutes the most supreme and excellent practice of a Bodhisattva.”
"For this reason, I should pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Mahākāśyapa, you have spoken these words well.
While the Buddha was thus praising Kāśyapa, twelve thousand beings in the assembly attained human and celestial bodies, and all of them resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:

"You should now know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses skillful means has already accomplished immeasurable merit; although they engage in activities at all times, they no longer give rise to those various unwholesome karmas, remaining free from faults regarding both themselves and others."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottama, having witnessed such events within the assembly of the Buddha and heard such teachings, again paid his respects and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?"
In the past, when he was a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood, within the Dharma of that Kāśyapa Tathāgata, he once spoke these words:
"For what reason do you shave your hair and beard?"
"How is it that while one seeks awakening, this awakening is most difficult to attain?
What was the meaning of those words spoken in the past?
I pray that the Buddha will now explain this to me."
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānottara:
"Stop, son of good family!
Do not speak such words."
It should be known that whatever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and whatever they teach is never without benefit. Why is this?

Because bodhisattvas who possess inconceivable skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) see various worthy beings and, according to what is appropriate for them to abide in, they discipline those various sentient beings as is fitting; one should know that all such actions do not depart from the skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Jñānottara!
I shall now explain to you in detail the profound, true Dharma of the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; you should listen attentively and apply your mind correctly."
"Good son! When I was formerly a bodhisattva, I accomplished inconceivable skillful means in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

At that time, within the Dharma of that Buddha, I realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). From that point onward, I became a bodhisattva who has attained this patience."

For the sake of awakening, they exert themselves with even greater diligence; whether for one eon or a hundred eons, they never grow weary, never feel revulsion or abandonment, and never lose mindfulness. Repeatedly returning to this realm of saṃsāra, they rescue and deliver sentient beings through skillful means. By the power of their own wisdom, they bring all their undertakings to fulfillment, yet they do not form the notion of dwelling even at the final limit; for the benefit of sentient beings, they never cease.
You should know that this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, son of good family, when I was a bodhisattva,

for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*), although I entered the śrāvaka’s samādhi of tranquility, and even entered the bodhisattva’s samādhi, whether in body or mind, I had no perception of emergence or submergence.
Although they have attained the bliss of tranquility, they do not dwell in or cling to it;

although they abide in samādhi, they remain diligent and untiring, teaching and transforming sentient beings through the six pāramitās and the four means of integration, never ceasing in any of their activities.
You should know that this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,

when I was a bodhisattva— having already attained the stage of being born only once more before buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and being about to realize the Way and turn the great wheel of Dharma— I observed reality as it is within the Tuṣita heaven palace:
"Should I now attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma here among these devas,
or among human beings?
Thus he observed, and further reflected:
"If I were to perform this benefit while remaining among the gods, the people of Jambudvīpa would not hear the Dharma;
if I were to perform this benefit while remaining in Jambudvīpa, these gods would not hear the Dharma."
"I shall now descend into Jambudvīpa as is appropriate for me to attain equal and perfect enlightenment; yet these devas may also be benefited.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflected and observed:

"If, after passing away from this Tuṣita heaven and descending to be born among humans, I were to manifest the signs of birth without entering a womb and attain perfect enlightenment in an instant, all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa would give rise to doubts:"
“From where has this Bodhisattva Śākyamuni come?
Has he come from among the devas,
or has he come from among the gandharvas?”
"Has he come through transformation?
For this reason, he vanished from among the devas and descended to Jambudvīpa, conforming to worldly ways by entering the womb of his mother.
You should know that this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,
although a bodhisattva dwells within the womb, sentient beings of the world should not conceive the notion that he dwells there in reality.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva originally arose with composure from the stainless and tranquil *samādhi*.

From passing away among the devas and descending into the human realm, to dwelling in the womb, taking birth, leaving home, and practicing austerities, up until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to achieve perfect awakening, subduing the hosts of Māra, and turning the great wheel of Dharma—all such deeds performed therein, the Bodhisattva remains pure and unstained, unmoving and unchanging, neither emerging nor sinking.

For this reason, it should be known that a bodhisattva of pure conduct does not truly dwell within the womb; one should know that this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, for what reason do Bodhisattvas manifest only birth from a womb and not other modes of birth?
It is because Bodhisattvas are the most supreme and most excellent among all sentient beings; they belong to the category of purity, being entirely unadulterated and singular.
By manifesting birth from a womb through such signs, one should know that this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, what are the signs when a bodhisattva first enters his mother’s womb?
That is to say:
when the Bodhisattva enters the mother’s womb, both internally and externally he is pure, peaceful, and free from difficulty; he experiences neither suffering nor affliction.

Just as he experienced pleasure while dwelling in the celestial realms in the past, so too is his experience of pleasant sensation when entering the mother’s womb. This is not like the manner of entry of worldly beings, who take up the impure and defiled *kalala* of their parents as the basis for entering the womb.
Furthermore, for what reason does the Bodhisattva dwell in the mother’s womb for a full ten months, neither more nor less?

It is because the Bodhisattva is not like worldly beings whose stay in the maternal womb may increase or decrease in the number of days and months; due to such increase or decrease, the womb would not be fully developed and the sense faculties would be deficient.
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva has fulfilled ten months, the fetal development is complete, all faculties are fully formed, and there is nothing increased or diminished.
One should know that this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, for what reason does the Bodhisattva not delight in palaces but instead takes birth in those groves?

It is because: for a long time, the Bodhisattva has remained far removed from clamor, delighting in secluded places and practicing the conduct of tranquility; he is constantly protected by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others.
The Bodhisattva desired that all the people of Kapilavastu might joyfully offer various incenses and flowers as an act of sympathetic rejoicing, and that each of them might behold him.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva was born within that grove.
Furthermore, for what reason was the Bodhisattva’s mother born with the Bodhisattva while grasping a branch of a tree?
It is said:
the mother of a Bodhisattva is not like any other worldly woman, who, at the time of childbirth, experiences painful sensations and undergoes great suffering.
When Queen Māyā gave birth to the Bodhisattva, she was endowed with pleasant sensations and experienced great bliss.
For this reason, the mother of the Bodhisattva climbed that tree branch and gave birth to the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, for what reason is it that a Bodhisattva, while in the mother’s womb, is able to recollect and know those three types of past events, and even knows all matters such as entering and dwelling in the womb?
That is to say:
the Bodhisattva Viśuddhacaryā is the most supreme and most excellent within the three realms; with right mindfulness manifest before him, he does not forget or lose any dharma whatsoever.
Therefore, although the Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, he is able to mindfully recollect and know all those matters.
Furthermore, for what reason did only Śakra, Lord of the Devas, come to provide protection at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth?
When the Bodhisattva was born, he was immediately received and held; at that time, were there no other devas or humans present?
It is said that Śakra, Lord of Devas, had previously made a great vow:
"When the Bodhisattva was born, he provided protection.
By the power of his past roots of virtue, it was for this reason that when the Bodhisattva was born, only Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to guard him.
Furthermore, for what reason did the Bodhisattva, immediately upon birth, take seven steps in each of the four directions— neither fewer than six nor more than eight?

It is because the supernatural transformations and skillful means of the Bodhisattva, the True Being, are such that, by virtue of these causes and conditions, he took exactly seven steps, with no increase or decrease.
Furthermore, for what reason did he, immediately after taking seven steps, utter these words:
"I am the most honored and most supreme in the world; I have already attained liberation from the conditions of old age, sickness, and death"?

This means that when the assembly of devaputras in this Brahma realm heard of the Bodhisattva’s birth, they all came to gaze upon him and pay their respects, each receiving benefit according to their own capacity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:
"Only the assembly of devaputras in this Brahma realm knows of this matter; I now wish to cause everyone everywhere to hear and know it."
Having formed this thought, he then uttered these words:
"I am the most honored and the most supreme in the world; I have already attained liberation from the laws of old age, sickness, and death."

When these words were spoken, all the hosts of devaputras and the hosts of Brahmās throughout the trichiliocosm, having heard this sound, arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva was in an instant; with palms joined in reverence, they rejoiced and offered praise.
For these reasons, he proclaimed these words:
"I am the most honored and the most supreme in the world.
