"Furthermore, noble son, for what reason does the Bodhisattva manifest a great laugh immediately upon birth?
Is it not because the Bodhisattva manifests this sign due to restlessness?"
That is to say:
once the Bodhisattva has been born, he reflects thus:
"I desire to cause all sentient beings everywhere to be able to resolve upon bodhicitta just as I have."
"Once I have attained awakening, I shall extensively deliver sentient beings from the suffering of saṃsāra; regarding this matter, I harbor no thought of indolence.
I observe that certain classes of sentient beings give rise to inferior minds and confused mental engagements, such that they are unable to initiate vast diligence upon the path to liberation."
What, then, is this? It is as follows:
those who possess the mind of great compassion are able to arouse diligence, whereas sentient beings of that [other] kind do not engage in such practice.
"I desire to cause them to achieve such vast diligence and attain the supreme liberation; for this reason, I take up the fruit of omniscience.
Due to these causes and conditions, joy arises in his mind, and he manifests a great smile because of that cause of joy, yet it is not a sign of the bodhisattva’s agitation.
"Furthermore, for what reason does the body of a Bodhisattva, which is fundamentally free from defilement, undergo bathing? It is said:
although the Bodhisattva has been free from stains and taints for immeasurable kalpas, in this present life, he bathes his body in accordance with worldly custom."
"Furthermore, for what reason did the Bodhisattva, after his birth, not immediately depart from the garden to proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and attain perfect awakening?
Why did he instead enter the royal palace? What was the purpose of this?"
That is to say:

the Bodhisattva’s physical marks are perfect and his majestic virtue is complete; all who behold him obtain benefit. Thus, the Bodhisattva enters the royal palace so that the court ladies and all his kinsmen may gaze upon him.
Furthermore, desiring to engage in worldly amusements within his palace and experience various pleasures—

though these involve activity yet lack any substantial reality— he renounced all possessions, including the rank of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), to leave the household life and cultivate the Way.
For these reasons, the Bodhisattva entered the royal palace once again.
Furthermore, for what reason did Queen Māyā pass away seven days after giving birth to the Bodhisattva?
Is this not the fault of the Bodhisattva? It is said:

when the Bodhisattva was about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to enter his mother’s womb, he first used his divine eye to observe with precision and saw that Queen Māyā’s lifespan would be fulfilled for ten months, after which she would reach the end of her life in seven days.
Having observed in this manner, the Bodhisattva entered the womb and remained there for ten months.
For this reason, Lady Māyā passed away seven days after his birth due to the exhaustion of her lifespan; it was not the fault of the Bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, before the Bodhisattva had gone forth from home, he studied all the worldly arts and skills, namely: writing, arithmetic, incantations, crafts, singing, dancing, and even matters such as archery and weaponry."
What is the meaning of training in this way? It is said:
it is because the Bodhisattva, desiring to discipline the world, manifests the most supreme state.

Why is this? Because within this trichiliocosm, there was not a single person whose learning or skill surpassed that of the Bodhisattva; for this reason, before he had left the household life, the Bodhisattva studied such matters.

"Furthermore, for what reason did the Bodhisattva, before he went forth from home, take a wife and have sons, and moreover possess a vast retinue of palace ladies, court beauties, and various kinsmen?"
Is it not the case that a bodhisattva gives rise to craving and attachment?
That is to say:
although a bodhisattva manifests such signs in common with the world, it is not that the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of craving and attachment.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already transcended craving and attachment; regarding all that he performs within the sphere of craving and attachment, there is no actual reality therein.
As for the Bodhisattva taking Yaśodharā as his wife, it was because the Bodhisattva wished to fulfill Yaśodharā’s long-cherished vow.
In the past, Yaśodharā made this vow before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, saying:
"May I become a woman of the Śākya clan within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha and plant various roots of goodness."
"Because she spoke no false words in her past lives, I have now accepted her as my wife so that she may quickly achieve the perfection of roots of goodness.
Although such is the way of worldly appearances, the Bodhisattva’s mind does not give rise to any fault; he will later renounce them, leave the household life, and cultivate the Way."
Regarding all those who give birth to sons such as Rāhula, people of the world speak thus in slander:
"If one has no offspring to continue the lineage through procreation, he is no true man."
Because the Bodhisattva stilled this slander, he caused Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, to give birth to the son Rāhula at that very moment.
One should know that this Rāhula was not born from the impurities of the parents' *kalala* and so forth, but rather descended from the celestial realm and manifested through transformational birth.

As for all the assembled palace ladies, handmaidens, and various kinsmen, the Bodhisattva, wishing to instruct and guide each according to their needs so that they might all attain the most supreme and beneficial merit, will subsequently renounce them to leave the household life and practice the Way.

Within his palace, the Bodhisattva taught and guided forty-two thousand palace ladies and maidservants through the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing them all to plant these roots of goodness for enlightenment;
as for the other palace women, they were merely able to develop pure faith and abide in right view.

Therefore, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path conform to worldly appearances—though they may dwell in royal palaces, take wives, have sons, and gather extensive retinues of palace ladies and kinsmen, even engaging in the play and enjoyment of the five desires—all their actions are devoid of substantial reality; they are pure and stainless, free from all defilements, without craving or attachment, and without movement or fluctuation.

The Bodhisattva acts solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming all sentient beings, in order to fulfill their past vows and bring their roots of goodness to maturity. Thus, through the power of inconceivable skillful means, supernormal knowledges, and vows, they manifest transformations and perform transformative deeds; within these playful displays of supernormal powers, they attain the tranquil bliss of samādhi, ensuring that whatever they do in accordance with circumstances brings benefit to all.

When the Bodhisattva dwelt in the royal palace, although he received all manner of elephants, horses, servants, and slaves, each and every one of them was due to his own extraordinary vow-power from previous lives; the Bodhisattva accepted them solely for the sake of fulfilling those vows.
For these reasons, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s taking of a wife and other such acts were not motivated by desire or attachment.
Furthermore, for what reason did the shadow of the Jambu tree not move even as the sun shifted when the Bodhisattva once went beneath it and sat cross-legged?
What are its characteristics?
They are as follows:
it is because the Bodhisattva desires to bring benefit to seven koṭis of devas and humans that its characteristics are thus.
Furthermore, for what reason does a Bodhisattva experience fear upon seeing old age, sickness, and death while wandering through gardens and groves? It is because,

although the Bodhisattva has already transcended the fears of old age, sickness, and death, he manifests such terror when seeing these signs in order to inspire in sentient beings a sense of wearying revulsion and dread toward cyclic existence.
Furthermore, for what reason did the Bodhisattva leave the city and renounce the household life during the middle watch of the night, rather than during the daytime?
It is said: the Bodhisattva chose the night so that all the people of Kapilavastu would not see him.

Furthermore, for the sake of causing the bodhisattva’s own roots of goodness to increase, his pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) to become purified, and them to be fully perfected, he renounces all pleasant things that he possesses.
Therefore, during the middle watch of the night, the Bodhisattva scaled the city wall and left the household life.
Furthermore, after the Bodhisattva had departed from the royal palace, he went to the place of asceticism and cut off his hair with his own hand.
When the Bodhisattva’s father, the Great King Śuddhodana, heard of these matters, he did not believe them, thinking:
"How could my son have cut off his hair?"
Later, when he realized the truth of the matter, his heart was filled with anguish.
What were these signs?
They were as follows:

The Bodhisattva, wishing that all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans throughout the trichiliocosm might behold the most supreme topknot of the Buddha’s auspicious and majestic light, and thereby obtain great benefit through gazing upon, prostrating to, and honoring it, cut off his own hair for this reason.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva was about to depart from the royal palace, he mounted the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka, who was adorned with various ornaments and driven by the charioteer Chandaka, who was skilled in guiding him.
At that time, the horse-king proceeded with joy, and subsequently cast off [the charioteer].
What are these signs?
They are as follows:

the Bodhisattva joyfully relinquishes all that is dear to him without any lingering attachment, desiring that all sentient beings in the final age may, like himself at this time, be free from all attachments and thus practice and study within my Dharma.

Furthermore, he caused those who have left the household life in the final age to do so by means of that right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) while studying the Path; for this reason, he abandoned the horse-king.

Again, for what reason did the Bodhisattva practice austerities for six years in a secluded place, undergoing various hardships? Is it not because of the remaining karmic obstructions of the Bodhisattva that he experienced such retribution?
That is to say:

the bodhisattva’s various hindrances have been exhausted, and there is no longer any retribution of suffering; all that he does is merely the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva. "Good son!..."
Regarding what you previously asked:
"When I was a Bodhisattva in my final birth before Buddhahood, I once spoke these words:
'For what reason do you shave your hair and beard?'"
"How is it that one seeks awakening, yet this awakening is most supreme and difficult to attain?
This causal condition is not without benefit; I shall now explain it to you as it truly is.

I recall that in the past, during the Dharma of Tathāgata Kāśyapa, I was a bodhisattva named Prabhāpāla; at that time, through skillful means, I brought benefit to all sentient beings according to what was appropriate for each.

At that time, there were five brahmins who were sons of noble families; they had previously practiced various pure conducts within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, but later, due to encountering those evil associates, they caused them to forget and lose their great bodhicitta.
At that very moment, those five brahmins gave rise to this thought:
"We have already attained the Dharma of Bodhi.
To give rise to such a thought is to be associated with heterodox views.
At that time, I perceived his mind through contemplation and, wishing to provide him with guidance by means of skillful means, spoke these words before him:
"For what reason have you shaved off your hair and beard?"
"How is it that one seeks bodhi, yet this bodhi is most supreme and difficult to attain?
When those five brahmins heard these words, they all thought to themselves:
"For what reason has the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatīputra spoken such words?"
I knew his thought and spoke to him again:
"For what reason have you shaved off your beard and hair?
How do you seek bodhi, which is the most supreme and difficult to attain?"
After I had spoken these words, I dwelt securely in the Dharma-gate of true equality and resided together with the five brahmins in one place.

At that time, two men—one named Kṛṣṇa and the other named Gopaka—came to where I and the five brahmins were. First, they extensively extolled the supreme merits of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa; subsequently, they spoke to me and the five brahmins, saying:
"Now we should go to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa.
At that time, I thought to myself:

"The roots of goodness of these five brahmins are not yet matured. If we were to go together now to the place of Buddha Kāśyapa, should I praise the supreme merits of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, those five brahmins would be unable to do so."
Having reflected thus, he said to those two men,
"I myself know the proper time.
Having spoken these words, I immediately dwelt in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) by dwelling in non-dwelling.
Protected by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he gave rise to skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and addressed the five brahmins, saying:
"I spoke to you earlier:
'For what reason have you shaved your hair and beards?'"
"How is it that one seeks bodhi, yet this bodhi is most difficult to attain?
You have not yet understood this meaning; I shall now explain it for you.
For what reason is bodhi difficult to attain? It is said:

if a bodhisattva has no conceptualization of practice and no conceptualization of abiding regarding the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), then they have neither knowledge nor attainment regarding bodhi; observing it as it truly is, they find nothing at all to be attained.

Furthermore, awakening (bodhi) is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind; in ultimate emptiness, there is nothing at all to be attained.
Therefore, I have previously said to you all:
"For what reason do you shave your hair and beard?
How do you seek bodhi, when this bodhi is most supreme and difficult to attain?"
"You should know that this teaching is the teaching of ultimate truth.
When the five brahmins heard this Dharma, their minds attained awakening, and they returned once more to abide within the Mahāyāna.
"Having spoken thus, I dwelt with a mind that finds nothing to be apprehended in any phenomena; I then departed from that place and went once more to another location."
At that time, those five brahmins were likewise staying in that same place.

Then, by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the two—Ghaṭikāra and Kuṇḍadhāna—went to that location and skillfully exhorted the five brahmins, leading them to go together to the abode of Kāśyapa Buddha.

At that time, having observed that the faculties and conditions of those five brahmins were already mature, I immediately went together with those five brahmins and the two others to the place where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa was.
Having arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, they each prostrated at the Buddha's feet.
At that time, by the power of their roots of goodness from previous lives, the two men beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs; thereupon, each attained purity of mind.

When those five brahmins beheld the Tathāgata’s physical marks, radiant light, auspiciousness, and majestic virtue, their hearts were filled with joy; by the power of the roots of goodness from their past lives, they each resolved once more to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, I addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The roots of goodness of these five brāhmaṇas have matured; I pray that the Buddha will transform and deliver them.

Then, Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, immediately expounded for them the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. According to their respective capacities, they were able to understand it, and immediately all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa then bestowed upon me the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having received this prediction, I addressed the Buddha Kāśyapa, saying:
"Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taken these five brāhmaṇas under his care, they have been enabled to see the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, he proclaimed for them the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, teaching and guiding them so that they might all attain patience; thus, these bodhisattvas seeking the Buddha’s bodhi would no longer regress. "Moreover, Jñānottama!
In the past, when I was a Bodhisattva in my final birth within the Dharma of that Tathāgata Kāśyapa, I previously spoke these words:
"For what reason do you shave your hair and beard?"

"How can one seek awakening when this awakening is so supremely difficult to attain?"—those who speak thus do so for the purpose of providing guidance; by means of these causes and conditions, they obtain benefit.
Therefore, you should know this:

whatever has been spoken is not without purpose or benefit; it is all the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and is neither a fault nor an unwholesome dharma (*akuśaladharma*).

"If there are sentient beings of little knowledge and little vision who, toward śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas pure in their observance of the precepts, utter meaningless speech—namely, claiming that what is wisdom is not wisdom—those who speak such words will be unable to bring benefit or peace for a long night, but will only encounter painful sensations."
These sentient beings commit unwholesome deeds; this is their fault.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is not like this: all obstructions and burdens have been completely purified, and not even the slightest trace of karmic obstruction remains. Rather, it is solely for the sake of extinguishing all evil dharmas for sentient beings and universally enabling them to become capable of realizing liberation.
Jñānottara! You should understand it thus according to past causes and conditions:
"Furthermore, all my six years of ascetic practice and endurance of various hardships were solely for the purpose of subduing the various non-Buddhists."
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to arouse diligence;
and by taking only a single sesame seed or a single grain of barley as food, he wishes to purify their physical vessels.
"By reason of these causes and conditions, I practiced various ascetic penances for six years, rather than as a karmic retribution for other deeds.
When I was thus practicing ascetic penances for six years in the past, five million hosts of devas and sages all attained the samādhi of wisdom and supernormal powers."
Therefore, you should know that I cultivated this practice for the sake of benefiting others through skillful means.
Furthermore, it was only after the Bodhisattva first accepted the milk-rice and his strength was replenished by eating it that he proceeded to the site of enlightenment to attain perfect awakening.
Why not simply allow his body to become emaciated and proceed to that place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to achieve perfect awakening?
That is to say:
out of compassion for all sentient beings in the final age, the Bodhisattva first accepted the milk-rice; only after eating it did he achieve perfect awakening.
Why is this? Because sentient beings in the final age all rely upon food and drink for their sustenance.
Among those sentient beings who seek the fruits of the Way, if they lack food and drink to support their bodies, they will be unable to progress and will all give rise to despondency and retreat.

If they obtain food and drink as sustenance, they will all attain peace and security; because of this peace and security, they will be able to keep all wholesome dharmas in mind, thereby being able to advance and seek the fruits of the Path.
I wish to cause those sentient beings of the final age to train in this way: that I first accept food and drink, and only thereafter proceed on the Path.
Furthermore, it is to enable the cowherd woman who offered the milk gruel to perfect the causes of her giving and to bring the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) to fulfillment.

At that time, having finished my meal, I sat peacefully at the site of enlightenment and attained the fruit of Bodhi; I was able to abide within a single samādhi for a thousand kalpas—all of this being sustained by the power of solid food—and for this reason, I accepted that milk-rice porridge.

Furthermore, once the Bodhisattva was seated upon the diamond throne beneath the Bodhi tree, why did he not immediately realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, but instead first subdue the various armies of Māra?
That is to say:
there is no place where the hosts of evil Māras can find accommodation.
If a bodhisattva does not accommodate them through skillful means, those evil Māras will then harass and disturb all sentient beings.
Therefore, once the Bodhisattva has taken his seat, he reflects thus:
"On this day I shall attain perfect enlightenment; among all the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, which beings are there whose minds do not rejoice?"
Having reflected thus, he observed that the various evil Māras were displeased and intended to cause harm to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further contemplated:
"I should not now engage in battle with the Māras; rather, I shall employ supernatural powers to perform transformations so as to bring them into submission."

Furthermore, having caused all the hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans to behold the Bodhisattva’s lion-like play of supernatural powers, they were inspired to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"For this reason, may all beings universally attain the supreme nirvana.

At that time, having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva immediately emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows; that light shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm, completely eclipsing all the palaces of Māra.
From within that light, this voice was uttered:

"Now this son of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan has renounced the rank of a universal monarch to leave the home life and practice the Way; he has proceeded to the site of enlightenment to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
When this sound was uttered, countless devas and humans from the fourfold assembly came to where the Bodhisattva was to gaze upon him, pay homage, and show reverence.

At that time, all the Māras and their retinues, having witnessed this event, fled in all directions; trembling with fear and alarm, the arrows of grief pierced their hearts, and they were overcome by great suffering and distress.

At that time, the host of evil Māras, their wrath increasing all the more, in an instant manifested fourfold armies that surrounded the site of enlightenment for a distance of one hundred yojanas on all sides, manifesting various transformations to cause disturbance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt in a mind of great loving-kindness; although he beheld these signs, he remained unmoved.
The Bodhisattva then formed the gesture of subduing Māra with his hands adorned with jeweled nets and garlands, and at that moment, all the Māras were immediately subdued.
At that time, eighty-four koṭis of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, you should know that the Bodhisattva’s prior manifestation of the signs of subduing Māra was entirely a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, for what reason did the Tathāgata, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remain seated in the full lotus posture for seven days and nights, gazing at that king of trees, silent and unmoving?
That is to say:

there were sons of gods in the realm of form who practiced the conduct of tranquility; seeing the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha sitting cross-legged, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they reflected thus:
"For seven days and nights, the Tathāgata has dwelt in tranquility, relying upon a single mind, yet this mind is ungraspable."
When he gave rise to this thought, thirty-two thousand devaputras from the realm of form (rūpadhātu) resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Desiring that all practitioners of the path in future ages might likewise cultivate such practice of tranquility, for this reason, after the Tathāgata had attained bodhi, he gazed at that king of trees for seven days and nights, remaining silent and unmoving.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment, for what reason did Brahmā first entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma?
The causal condition for this is that the assembly of Brahmās entreated their King to teach the Dharma according to the needs of beings.

Why is this? Those Brahmā hosts believe they rely upon the Brahmā King, and they further believe that the Brahmā King can produce them; thus, in this world, there is none who is prior to or superior to the Brahmā King.
At that time, Brahmā made this reflection:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is the Honored One of the world; he is able to know the faculties of all sentient beings according to their needs.
Therefore, I should entreat him to preach the Dharma."
Having formed this thought, he went to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and exhorted the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of the true Dharma.
While that Brahmā King was thus exhorting him, six million eight hundred thousand members of the Brahma assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Brahma King was the first to entreat the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma. Furthermore, O Jñānottara!
The Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom can fully illuminate the speech and mental activities of all sentient beings; there is nothing among all their deeds that it does not accommodate.

It illuminates and perceives the initial limits of sentient beings—those who possess roots of goodness and those who do not—and the various karmic retributions of each and every being are all clearly manifested within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Even the responsive manifestations and rewards enacted by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas appear therein: the Bodhisattva proceeding to the site of enlightenment to achieve equal and perfect awakening; the fulfillment of all pure dharmas and supreme merits; the Tathāgata having severed all unwholesome states, having purified all obstructions and burdens, and having distanced himself from all faults—all such merits are fully revealed and illuminated by the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
"Furthermore, Jñānottara! The Tathāgata, arising from a heart of great compassion, employs skillful means to universally deliver all sentient beings.

It is like a physician who is well-versed in medicine; for all those who are ill, he prepares excellent medicines by blending sweet, bitter, and pungent flavors according to their specific instructions, administering them in accordance with each disease so that all may be cured."

The Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, is likewise so: endowed with all manner of skillful means, he acts as a great king of physicians who skillfully cures all ailments. Observing whatever illness each sentient being may have, he provides healing through appropriate skillful means, causing them all to attain liberation.

"Furthermore, it is like a newborn infant in this world, whom a compassionate mother nourishes with her milk, raising him with kindness and affection so that he is not afflicted by even the slightest suffering or illness."
If later they fall ill, a compassionate mother will immediately select excellent medicine for them and give it to them to take; once the child has taken it, they attain peace and well-being.

The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is likewise so: he is the father of all the world, regarding all sentient beings with the thought that they are his own children, never allowing any being to suffer affliction.

If the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings creating various karmas and receiving their respective retributions, he employs skillful means according to their needs to deliver them and enable their liberation.
Jñānottara! You should know that what has been thus explained constitutes skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
This concludes the third fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-upāyakauśalya-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Skillful Means, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
"Furthermore, Jñānottara!
I recall that in a past age, there were five hundred merchants who entered the ocean to seek jewels.
At that time, there was another merchant whose nature was rigid, fierce, and violent; he suddenly encountered them on the way across the sea."
That merchant immediately conceived an evil thought, intending to plot for the precious treasures.
He reflected to himself:
"I should now employ a skillful means to take the lives of all these merchants; having done so, I shall take the treasures and return to Jambudvīpa to enjoy happiness for myself."

At that time, among the assembly of five hundred merchants, there was a caravan leader named Sārthavāha (Good Driver). He was compassionate and gentle by nature, and he constantly gave rise to feelings of pity and mercy toward all people.
Once, while the merchant leader was resting and lying down, he suddenly saw the deity of the great ocean appear in a dream and address him, saying:
"Merchant leader, you should know that among the caravan there is one person apart from the rest, who is violent and evil by nature, possessing such physical appearance and such a name."
That person gave rise to a mind of malice and intended to plot for the precious treasures, thinking to himself:
"I should quickly take the lives of all these merchants, seize their precious treasures, and return to Jambudvīpa to enjoy happiness for myself."

Therefore, I have now spoken to you first according to what I have reflected; you should consider what skillful means can be employed so that this evil man does not commit the karma of killing, thereby avoiding the retribution of hell, and furthermore, so that the merchant caravan may preserve their lives.

Why is this? Because these five hundred merchants have all already established themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are irreversible; if that evil person commits an act of killing against such a one who abides in the Dharma of a bodhisattva, he will fall eternally into hell with no prospect of escape.
"Therefore, you should now employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them well.
At that time, the merchant leader Sudhana, having awakened from his dream, immediately thought to himself:
"What skillful means can I employ at this moment so that these wicked men do not commit the karma of killing, escape the retribution of hell, and allow all the merchants to preserve their lives?"
Thus he reflected for one day, seeking skillful means, yet was unable to find them; even after reflecting with meticulous attention for seven days, he still could not find them.
After seven days had passed, he thought to himself:
"I now have no further means available; I must first take the life of those who harbor murderous intent toward me."
"Because he has taken life, he shall not create the karma of killing and will thus escape the retribution of hell; furthermore, it will cause the rest of the multitude to preserve their lives.
Having thought this, he further deliberated:
"If I were to join these five hundred merchants in taking his life, all five hundred would fall into hell."
"I should now give rise to a heart of great compassion; for the sake of rescue and protection, I shall kill with my own hands.
As for this cause of killing, even if I must undergo retribution in the hells for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I shall endure it."

However, by means of such great compassion and skillful expedients at this very moment, you can cause these evil men not to commit the karma of killing, so that they may avoid the immeasurable suffering of hell for countless kalpas;
furthermore, you can ensure that the assembly of merchants who abide in the Bodhisattva-dharma remain secure and free from calamity.
At that time, having formed this thought, the merchant leader employed a skillful means and took his life.
Thereupon, that wicked man, upon the end of his life, was reborn in the celestial realm.
“Jñānottara! You should know that those five hundred merchants were none other than the five hundred Tathāgatas of this Bhadrakalpa;
the one who was the caravan leader among that assembly at that time was myself.”
Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas in saṃsāra, I have generated skillful means through great compassion and thus rescued sentient beings in these various ways.
What do you think?

Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may remain within saṃsāra for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is entirely for the sake of saving sentient beings through the wisdom of skillful means; one must not say that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses any karmic obstructions.

Therefore, you should know that all the deeds performed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are entirely pure, such that not even the slightest trace of obstruction or defilement can be found. "O Jñānottara!

Furthermore, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a vajra-like indestructible body; even his lifting and lowering of his feet perform great benefit through the skillful means of supernatural power.

At that time, there were twenty people in the city of Śrāvastī who suddenly encountered twenty extremely evil associates. These individuals conceived malicious intentions toward one another, desiring to plot their mutual murder, and each sought out various means to carry it out.
At that time, the forty men, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual strength, went together to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they stood to one side.

Then, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desiring to transform and deliver those forty men, manifested in an instant a great person within the assembly and addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Venerable One, you should know that before long, various signs of grasses and trees will appear upon this great earth.”
Then that Great Being spoke these words:
"At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately extended his right foot.
In an instant, this great earth produced grasses and trees, each measuring one chi in height.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these signs of grasses and trees that have now appeared, might I see them in other regions?”
The Buddha said,
“I cannot. Thereupon,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately took a small amount of grass and wood and held it himself.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in its entirety.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested his own form so as to transcend the Brahma realm, and these grasses and trees likewise followed him out beyond the Brahma realm;
furthermore, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested himself within the great ocean, and these grasses and trees likewise stayed there with him.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal power, entered among the great mountains, these grasses and trees likewise remained there with him.
At that time, once the Tathāgata had returned to his original seat and withdrawn his right foot, these grasses and trees likewise remained settled and unmoving.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did the Tathāgata manifest this sign in the past?”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
In the past, I was a great merchant leader who entered the sea to seek jewels. I encountered an evil friend, and at that time, out of a heart of great compassion, I took his life.”

"Due to past causes and conditions, there is now this sign. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "This sign now manifested does not abide In the void, nor in mountains or seas; It is not within the earth, nor in the waters, Nor does it dwell within the bodies of beings. This sign has no fixed location; It is not found within the ten directions. The Buddhas of the three times have all attained enlightenment By relying on the Dharma-nature, which is without abode.

Just as space pervades everywhere Yet has no specific place of dwelling, So too do the Buddhas of the three times Rely upon the Dharma-nature to attain the Way. The Dharma-nature is inherently quiescent and empty; It is neither born nor extinguished. Because they have realized this nature, All Buddhas have attained the Way. If one can contemplate the Dharma-nature With a mind free from attachment, One will surely realize the fruit of Buddhahood And transcend the suffering of birth and death."
"Even though he does not abide in any place, he abides in this manner due to past causes.
At that time, those forty people all thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata is the Great Dharma King; no actual karmic obstacles can be found in him."
"We have harbored evil intentions toward one another and plotted to harm each other; now, in the presence of the Buddha, we ought to repent.
Having thought this, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We previously gave rise to evil intentions, desiring to kill one another.
Therefore, at this time, we each repent.
At that moment, the World-Honored One preached the essentials of the Dharma to them according to their needs, and those forty people all attained the samādhi of realization through wisdom.
At that time, three million two hundred thousand sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

"Jñānottara! By this cause and condition, you should know that every lifting and lowering of the feet by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is a supernatural skillful means that brings about great benefit; truly, there is not even the slightest karmic obstruction to be found."
"Furthermore, since the Tathāgata is already free from all ailments, for what purpose did he once dispatch the bhikṣus to Jīvaka’s place to seek the juice of blue lotus stamens?
What was the necessity for this?"
It is said:

At one time, not long after I had entered the rains retreat with five hundred bhikṣus, we were dwelling in a forest grove. At that time, there was a practitioner of the *vāmalomavika* (left-hair) asceticism living on the edge of that forest.

If this person should suddenly fall ill, being unable to move or remain still and unable to subdue the affliction, they will then seek me out to request a wondrous medicine to rescue them from their suffering.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"I should not now concern myself with what is appropriate for this illness. Why is that?
If I were to know what is appropriate for their illness, I would later, in the final age, destroy the noble mind [of others].
What skillful means can I now employ to obtain medicine and provide treatment?
I shall simply cause this assembly of bhikṣus to seek that medicine on my behalf.
Having formed this thought, he immediately ordered the bhikṣus to go to Jīvaka’s place to request the juice of blue lotus stamens for the treatment of his illness.
Although these bhikṣus received the Buddha’s command, they did not act upon it immediately.
At that time, the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, having seen the bhikṣus, addressed them, saying:
"Venerable ones!
You should act according to the Buddha’s instructions and seek such medicine as will provide a remedy; do not seek another medicine that would cause him to pass away after he has taken it."
The bhikṣus said:
"If we were to go out to seek medicine and thereby violate the Buddha’s precepts and Dharma, we would rather lose our own lives than ever act in violation of the Buddha’s precepts and Dharma."
The Śuddhāvāsa devaputra addressed the bhikṣus again, saying:
"The Tathāgata is the Great Dharma King; out of a heart that seeks to benefit others, he manifests these signs like taking medicine to eliminate illness."
"Why do you not now act according to the instruction?
You must go and seek the medicine; you must go and seek the medicine.
After the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven had spoken thus three times, the bhikṣus set aside their doubts and remorse, and immediately went to Jīvaka’s place to seek such medicine.
Having obtained this medicine, I gave it to that patient, who was cured after taking it. O Jñānottara!
For this reason, and for the sake of benefiting others, I dispatched bhikṣus to seek such medicine; it is not that the Tathāgata has any illness or affliction.
Furthermore, among all the accumulations of merit of the Tathāgata, which are most supreme and most excellent, for what reason does he first take up his alms-bowl and enter the city to beg for food?
It is said:

The Tathāgata has already transcended all obstacles and no longer possesses the notion of substantial food; yet, out of compassion for those bhikṣus in the future末法 (final age) who possess little merit—those who, though they enter royal cities and villages with their bowls to beg for food, are unable to obtain it and thus give rise to despondency, being unable to persevere in the practice of begging for long periods—he acts in this way.
To cause these bhikṣus to reflect at that time:

"Even the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, who possesses the most supreme accumulation of merit among all in the world, still wanders for alms with a bowl as appropriate; how much more so for us, the bhikṣus of this final age, whose merit and virtue are meager? Since begging for food is difficult, we should not give rise to suffering."
"One should simply go on alms-round; even if one obtains but little, it shall suffice. "Jñānottara!

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata goes on alms-round while in the world, he does so for the sake of conforming to and benefiting others. That is to say, by means of the empowerment of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he causes all the brahmins, elders, householders, and indeed all people, to have abundant food and drink in this present life, so that they do not encounter the suffering of famine."
Why is this? While the Tathāgata remains in the world, he does not allow the various māras to create the calamity of famine.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, through skillful means in accordance with the world, partakes of solid food without giving rise to attachment; nor does he cause the brahmins, householders, or even all the people and the hosts of other devaputras to conceive such thoughts as these:
“The śramaṇa Gautama applies his attention with craving toward edible food.

In order to prevent such thoughts from arising in them, the Tathāgata, throughout the day and night, remains constantly in samādhi with the community of bhikṣus; relying on a single mind, he is tranquil and unmoving, without elevation or depression, the former following the latter and the latter like the former, in constant association with right mindfulness.

At one time, while I was dwelling in samādhi, seventy thousand devaputras gave rise to pure faith and paid homage to me. I immediately emerged from samādhi and, for their sake, proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma as was appropriate; those devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
For this reason, you should know that when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, practice begging for alms, they do so solely as a skillful means to bring about benefit.
Furthermore, at one time there was a Caṇḍāla-Māṇavaka who conceived an evil intent toward the Buddha, the Tathāgata, and was destined to fall into hell; how did the Buddha protect him?
That is to say:

the Tathāgata is equal toward enemies and kin, such that not even the slightest trace of obstruction or affliction can be found; he acts solely for the peace, happiness, and benefit of sentient beings.

At that time, desiring to rescue and protect that Caṇḍamāṇavaka, I employed my sovereign spiritual power (*vibhūti*) to cause him to behold the Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā in various worlds; within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of those Tathāgatas, the actions performed by that [being] were manifested.
By the supernatural power of the Tathāgatas, this māṇavaka, having seen his own karma, immediately gave rise to a mind of repentance and spoke these words:
"Now, within this very place, reality has been clearly revealed; I reflect upon how the Tathāgata is fully endowed with all pure dharmas."
"Why is it that I have now only created evil karma and am unable to attain a portion of the pure dharmas?

While that māṇavaka was thinking this, he immediately attained the pure and perfectly white brahmacarya. In his dream, he beheld the manifestation of the Buddha's body; all the sins arising from his previous malicious intentions were completely extinguished, and after his life ended, he was spared from retribution in the hells.
You should know that all this is due to the Tathāgata’s supernatural power providing protection and refuge. Why is this? It is because:
Because the Tathāgata, through the skillful means of great compassion, does not abandon sentient beings.
Furthermore, on one occasion, there was a brahmin named Sunakṣatra in the Jeta Grove; he took his own life due to certain causes and conditions.
At that time, one might wonder how the Buddha can be called "All-Knowing" (Sarvajña) if he does not know [this]. It is said:

the Tathāgata is fully endowed with unimpeded, correct knowledge; there is nothing he does not know or see. Regarding all matters such as various physical forms and supernormal powers, the Tathāgata establishes them all through his majestic spiritual power.
As for this brahmin Sunāri, the Buddha has observed that his lifespan is exhausted and that his death is certain; it is not that the Tathāgata is unable to know this.
Furthermore, wishing by these causes and conditions to subdue the minds of the various non-Buddhists and cause them to cease their own transgressions,
the Tathāgata, through his power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), did not enter a village for seven nights.
At that time, sixty koṭis of devas and humans, having passed seven nights, went to where the Buddha was.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, he preached the essentials of the Dharma to them according to their needs; immediately, each of them attained the samādhi of realized wisdom.
Furthermore, for what reason did the Tathāgata formerly consume horse barley for three months?
It was because the Tathāgata wished to inspire a sense of wonder in the brahmins, householders, and others, and also to accomplish matters of benefit.
Why is this so? Once, while I was with five hundred bhikṣus, I saw five hundred horses; I observed that the roots of goodness those horses had cultivated in previous lives had now reached maturity.

Why is this? These five hundred horses were once human beings in previous lives; they drew near to and made offerings to former Tathāgatas, and in the presence of those former Buddhas, they gave rise to the bodhicitta. Later, however, because they encountered evil associates who destroyed their wholesome dharmas and caused them to commit various evil deeds, they now undergo the bodies of horses as a result of that karmic retribution.

Furthermore, these five hundred horses had previously made great vows before the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha; by the power of those past vows, they have now encountered the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha again, who has taught them through skillful means of the Dharma of Bodhi, enabling them to attain liberation.
"Because of the Bodhisattva’s majestic power and the force of their own vows, these five hundred horses were each able to recollect the events of their past lives.

Jñānottara! Observing those horses and seeing these causes and conditions, I gave rise to a heart of compassion and a desire to transform and deliver them; thus, together with the bhikṣus, I went to where the horses were and took the barley they were eating to feed to them."
After I had eaten myself, I gave it to those five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, because of the power of their past roots of goodness, the five hundred horses saw the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus eating this horse-barley; they immediately prostrated before the Buddha and the various bhikṣus.

After three months had passed, those five hundred horses all died and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven; they then came from that heaven to the place where the Buddha was, paying him homage, honoring him, revering him, and making offerings to him.
The Buddha then taught the essentials of the Dharma according to their capacities, and all these sons of gods became established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* at the stage of non-retrogression.
It was for the sake of bringing such great benefit to these five hundred horses that the Tathāgata ate horse-barley.
“Jñānottara, you should know that whatever food and drink the Tathāgata consumes is the most supreme food.
Even if the earth and molasses of a trichiliocosm were consumed by the Tathāgata, these two kinds would be equal and without distinction, both becoming the most excellent flavor.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s tongue-root always attains the supreme flavor; this is a mark of a Great Man.
For this reason, one should know that whatever food the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, receive is always the most excellent food.
At that time, I said to Ānanda:
"You have renounced the throne of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and cultivate the Way, giving rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings.
What flavor do you find in eating this horse-barley now?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These horse-barley grains are truly rare; although I was born in the royal palace, I have never before obtained such a supreme flavor.”
"At that time, Ānanda, having eaten the horse-barley, attained great joy and bliss for seven days. 'O Jñānottara!
At that time, after I and those five hundred bhikṣus had completed the summer retreat, we each returned to our respective dwellings.'"

At that time, among the assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, there were forty bhikṣus who ate this horse-barley; although they formed a perception of purity regarding its flavor, they still continued to long for various coarse and bitter foods.
Having reflected thus, each of them attained the fruit of Arhatship within seven nights.
"Jñānottara, you should know that although the Tathāgata ate horse barley, this was truly not a matter of retribution for past obstacles;
rather, it was for the sake of bringing great benefit to sentient beings, and to cause those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who cultivate pure precepts to give rise to a sense of rare wonder."
Furthermore, he causes all sentient beings to be able to act according to what they have been taught.
One should know that the Tathāgata is supreme in all respects, and that all his deeds do not violate the course of the Dharma.
Moreover, for what reason did the Tathāgata at one time say to Kāśyapa:
"I am suffering from back pain; you should explain the Dharma of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment for me.
Regarding this causal condition, it is as follows:
at that time, eight thousand devaputras had gathered together.

These sons of the gods had not yet given rise to pure faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; however, upon hearing Kāśyapa briefly explain the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment at that time, their faith was gradually able to awaken.
They immediately went to where Kāśyapa was, and Kāśyapa again extensively analyzed and explained the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) for them.
At that moment, those eight thousand devaputras each attained the samādhi of realization through wisdom (*jñānasākṣātkriyā-samādhi*), and they reflected to themselves:
"Sentient beings who are afflicted by illness cannot listen to the Dharma; yet if they hear the Dharma, their illnesses will be eliminated."
The Tathāgata is the Great Dharma King; even so, he manifests illness to cause Mahākāśyapa to preach the Dharma of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
How could we not delight in hearing the Dharma?
After those devaputras had reflected thus, their minds attained purity regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Because of this causal benefit, the Tathāgata manifested back pain and had Mahākāśyapa preach the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment.
"You should know that all of this is a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and is not, in reality, a matter of retribution for past obstacles.
Furthermore, for what reason did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, not give rise to anger or resentment at that time when the brahmin *Vyūha-dhvaja* once addressed him with unwholesome words?"
That is to say:

the Tathāgata, within the great assemblies of the fourfold community of devas and humans, has already attained patience and is fully endowed with the powers; thus, as he contemplates all objects of perception, he gives rise to neither anger nor obstruction.
At that time, the Tathāgata dwelt toward all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity, a mind of protection, a mind of stability, a mind of gentleness, and a mind of valor.
While the Tathāgata dwelt in these various states of mind, four thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because of these beneficial causes, the Tathāgata did not give rise to anger or obstruction toward the brahmin Vyūhadhvaja.
One should know that this was entirely the Tathāgata’s skillful means, and was truly not a matter of retribution for past karmic obstacles.
"Furthermore, Jñānottara!
I recall that in the past, when I was a bodhisattva, Devadatta constantly followed me wherever I went. Why was this? "

Although that Devadatta came to my presence seeking to harass and harm me, he was able to cause me to fulfill the six *pāramitās* and to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings. That is to say, whenever I wished to cause sentient beings to attain great happiness, yet I was unable to practice the dharma of gathering them through giving, Devadatta would come to me and beg for my wife and children, my slaves and servants, or even my head, eyes, hands, and feet; at those times, I was able to relinquish them all.
Because they are able to renounce, they say:
"This is called a practice that is difficult to perform; it can cause sentient beings to give rise to roots of goodness.
When I made this offering, immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to hearts of love and joy, attaining pure faith and understanding in the practice of giving.
Furthermore, at another time, when I was abiding in the practice of pure precepts through the power of my bodhicitta vow, Devadatta came to me with the intent to destroy those pure precepts.
At that time, I remained firm and unshakable, not violating my conduct of the precepts.
When immeasurable sentient beings saw this, they all came to abide in the ground of pure precepts.
Furthermore, whenever Devadatta gave rise to anger toward me, or struck or reviled me, at those times I did not harbor resentment, but remained in a mind of patience.
When immeasurable sentient beings saw this event, they all abided in the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).

Through Devadatta, I have brought to perfection all practices such as diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), and have enabled immeasurable sentient beings to attain great benefit.
"Jñānottara! You should know that although Devadatta sought to cause me harm, he was able to cause me to increase in wholesome dharmas and perform deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Therefore, one should know that because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, employ skillful means, whatever they perform for sentient beings ensures that all their karmic retributions remain unimpaired.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata universally observes the realm of sentient beings; seeing that certain sentient beings create such causes and receive such retributions, he employs various skillful means to transform and deliver them according to what he has observed.

“Jñānottara! As I have previously stated, all these various Dharma gates are the most supreme skillful means; such Dharma gates should not be preached before those who possess inferior roots of goodness.”

Why is this? Although all sentient beings may plant roots of goodness corresponding to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they are nonetheless unable to practice and study according to principle within these most supreme skillful means.
Why is this? Because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
One should only expound the teachings of the Bodhisattva path to those who are practicing it in accordance with reality.
For example, a person born blind, even if there is light during the night, cannot perceive any visual objects;
whereas a person with sight, during that same night, being illuminated by that light, is able to clearly observe all visual objects.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having already cultivated the most supreme practices of a bodhisattva and being further endowed with skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), they are able to fully penetrate all the supreme practices of the Buddhas and all the gateways to liberation (vimokṣa-mukha).

“Jñānottara! If there are sons or daughters of good family who aspire to unsurpassed bodhi, because they delight in the Dharma, even if such a place where this skillful means dharma-gate is being proclaimed lies hundreds or thousands of yojanas away, they will not be afraid of the distance but will immediately come to hear and receive it.”
Why is this? Because if a person hears this Dharma, they immediately attain vast radiance, their conduct becomes pure, and they are freed from all doubt and regret regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, you should know that among all the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, those who are vessels of the Dharma will be able to take joy in hearing and receiving this teaching;
whereas those who are not vessels of the Dharma, though they may hear it, will not give rise to such joy.
When the Buddha had spoken this Dharma, seventy-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This is called ‘The True Dharma of Skillful Means Pāramitā,’ and it is also called ‘The True Dharma of the Supreme Secret All-Pervading Pāramitā.’”
"You should receive and uphold this title, and in the future, during the final age, propagate and disseminate it so that all sentient beings may obtain great benefit.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda and the other śrāvakas, Jñānavatī and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the entire assembly—including the devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas of the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Skillful Means Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
